questions.stem: An older adult who is bedbound, intermittently incontinent, and eating poorly has a Braden Scale score that falls from 20 on admission to 14 today. Which nursing interpretation is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The score change is not clinically meaningful unless a pressure injury is already visible, so routine skin care should continue without changing the prevention plan.","B":"The lower score indicates greater pressure-injury risk and should prompt reassessment of individual risk factors and a more intensive, tailored prevention plan.","C":"The lower score indicates improved mobility and tissue tolerance, so preventive interventions can be reduced while the nurse continues daily skin inspection.","D":"The score alone determines the exact prevention bundle, so the nurse should apply the same standardized interventions to every client who scores 14."}}
questions.rationale: A lower Braden Scale score indicates higher pressure-injury risk. AHRQ recommends using validated risk assessment together with other clinical risk factors to plan targeted prevention rather than relying on the score alone.
questions.source_name: AHRQ — Preventing Pressure Ulcers in Hospitals
questions.source_detail: AHRQ states that lower Braden scores indicate higher risk and that risk scores should be combined with individual clinical assessment to guide preventive care.

questions.stem: A client with chronic diarrhea has a magnesium level of 1.1 mEq/L, new tremor and hyperreflexia, and frequent premature ventricular contractions. Which interpretation is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The findings suggest hypermagnesemia because excess magnesium increases neuromuscular excitability and commonly produces premature ventricular contractions.","B":"The magnesium value is within the expected adult range today, so the tremor and ventricular ectopy should be evaluated as unrelated findings.","C":"The findings are consistent with hypomagnesemia causing neuromuscular and cardiac excitability and warrant prompt clinical evaluation and correction.","D":"The findings primarily indicate hypocalcemia because magnesium depletion does not independently increase the risk of ventricular dysrhythmias."}}
questions.rationale: Hypomagnesemia can produce neuromuscular hyperexcitability and dysrhythmias, including premature ventricular beats and more serious ventricular arrhythmias.
questions.source_detail: Current NCBI clinical review identifies tremor/hyperreflexia and ventricular premature systoles/arrhythmias among manifestations of magnesium deficiency.

questions.stem: An unconscious client with an absent gag reflex requires oral hygiene. Secretions are pooling in the mouth, and suction equipment is available. Which positioning plan best reduces aspiration risk during care?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Keep the client supine with the head flat so oral secretions remain visible and can be removed before they move toward the pharynx.","B":"Place the client in Trendelenburg so gravity keeps oral fluid away from the lower airway while the mouth is cleaned and suctioned.","C":"Sit the client fully upright without head support because a 90-degree position eliminates aspiration risk even when airway reflexes are absent.","D":"Elevate the head when feasible, turn the head to the side or use a lateral position, and keep suction available to remove pooled secretions."}}
questions.rationale: For an unconscious patient receiving oral care, the head should be elevated and turned to the side; aspiration-risk care also requires attention to pooled secretions and suction when needed.
questions.source_name: NCBI Bookshelf — Assisting Patients With Personal Hygiene
questions.source_detail: NCBI guidance for oral hygiene in an unconscious patient recommends head elevation of about 45 degrees or more with the head turned to the side.
